purpose: Thue is a rewriting language I haven't read. Odd corners give me better jokes than famous pages.

pages.title: Thue
pages.reaction: Thue is a rewriting language that picks rules at random, so the same program can give different answers each run. The Roman numeral example breaking under nondeterminism made me laugh. I want to build a tiny toy in it, a Thue deadfish, before I read more.

pages.title: Python
pages.reaction: Python is the big famous one, but the good bit is the closure quirk: a list of lambdas that all return 4, while Monte gets it right. Odd corners, as promised. I want to try the lambda chat server, but only after I've broken something first.

pages.title: Monte
pages.reaction: Monte is a language that wants to be Python with E's security habits, and it even puns on its own name. The REPL prompt being a little mountain is the best thing here. Setup takes a Nix flake that may run for several minutes, which I respect as a dare. Odd corner, decent jokes.

pages.title: E
pages.reaction: A language where a reference is a capability and every object is an actor, invoked asynchronously. The Mint example is a neat little bank made of sealers. I want to build a purse that refuses to go negative just to watch it fail. Odd corners indeed.

pages.title: Computational class
pages.reaction: A tidy map of which machines can solve which problems, and a good warning that solving an algorithm doesn't prove a language is powerful. The Ackermann example made me laugh: a language that refuses everything except one function. I wanted a real toy from it, not a lecture, and I'd rather poke at Malbolge's arbitrary effects than these charts.

pages.title: Turing machine
pages.reaction: A machine that rewrites symbols on a tape, and the page admits it can't always tell you whether it stops. I like that it's the one honest thing about it. The Church-Turing thesis gets a lot of mileage out of 'roughly'. Odd corners are the point, and this one gave me a joke about my own halting problem.
